questions.question: The number of distinct eigenvalues of the matrix \[A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 & 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\] is equal to .
questions.explanation:
\[A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 & 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\] The matrix \(A\) is an upper triangular matrix because all entries below the main diagonal are zero. Hence, the eigenvalues are the elements of principle diagonal. \[\lambda_1 = 2, \quad \lambda_2 = 1, \quad \lambda_3 = 3, \quad \lambda_4 = 2\] \[\text{Distinct eigenvalues} = \{1, 2, 3\}\] The total number of distinct eigenvalues is 3. \[\boxed{3}\]
Key points
  • For triangular, or diagonal matrices, the eigenvalues are the diagonal elements.

questions.question: The value of the integral \(\int_{0}^{\pi} \int_{y}^{\pi} \frac{\sin x}{x} dx dy\), is equal to .
questions.explanation:
The given integral is \(I = \int_{0}^{\pi} \int_{y}^{\pi} \frac{\sin x}{x} \, dx \, dy\).
  • Initial Limits: The integration order \(dx \, dy\) has limits \(y \leq x \leq \pi\) and \(0 \leq y \leq \pi\).
  • Change of Order: Since \(\int \frac{\sin x}{x} \, dx\) is non-elementary, we switch to \(dy \, dx\). The triangular region bounded by \(x = y\), \(x = \pi\), and \(y = 0\) gives new limits: \(0 \leq y \leq x\) and \(0 \leq x \leq \pi\).
  • Setup: The integral becomes: \[I = \int_{0}^{\pi} \int_{0}^{x} \frac{\sin x}{x} \, dy \, dx\]
  • Inner Integration: Integrating with respect to \(y\): \[I = \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\sin x}{x} \Big[ y \Big]_{0}^{x} \, dx = \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\sin x}{x} \cdot x \, dx = \int_{0}^{\pi} \sin x \, dx\]
  • Final Evaluation:
    \[I = \Big[ -\cos x \Big]_{0}^{\pi} = -(\cos \pi - \cos 0) = -(-1 - 1) = 2\]
\[\boxed{2}\]
Key points
  • Changing the order of integration simplifies problems where the inner function lacks a standard antiderivative.
  • The region is a triangle with vertices \((0,0)\), \((\pi,0)\), and \((\pi,\pi)\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Ensure the constant limits (\(0\) to \(\pi\)) are moved to the outer integral during the swap.
  • Do not attempt to use the Taylor series for \(\frac{\sin x}{x}\) unless specifically asked, as changing the order is more efficient.

questions.question: Consider a differentiable function \(f(x)\) on the set of real numbers such that \(f(-1) = 0\) and \(|f'(x)| \leq 2\). Given these conditions, which one of the following inequalities is necessarily true for all \(x \in [-2, 2]\)?
questions.explanation: By Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem (LMVT), for any \(x \in [-2, 2]\) (\(x \neq -1\)), there exists some \(c\) between \(-1\) and \(x\) such that: \[\frac{f(x) - f(-1)}{x - (-1)} = f'(c)\] Given that \(f(-1) = 0\), this simplifies to: \[\frac{f(x)}{x + 1} = f'(c)\] Taking the absolute value on both sides: \[\frac{|f(x)|}{|x + 1|} = |f'(c)|\] Since \(|f'(x)| \leq 2\) for all real numbers, it follows that \(|f'(c)| \leq 2\): \[\frac{|f(x)|}{|x + 1|} \leq 2 \implies |f(x)| \leq 2|x + 1|\] Using the property that any real number is less than or equal to its absolute value (\(f(x) \leq |f(x)|\)): \[f(x) \leq 2|x + 1|\] For \(x = -1\), the inequality holds trivially (\(0 \leq 0\)). Thus, the statement is necessarily true for all \(x \in [-2, 2]\). \[\boxed{\text{(c)}\ \ f(x) \le 2|x+1|}\]

questions.question: Consider the line integral \[\int_C (x\,dy-y\,dx)\] the integral being taken in a counterclockwise direction over the closed curve \(C\) that forms the boundary of the region \(R\) shown in the figure below. The region \(R\) is the area enclosed by the union of a \(2\times 3\) rectangle and a semi-circle of radius \(1\). The line integral evaluates to
questions.explanation:
Given line integral \[\oint_C (x\,dy-y\,dx)\] where \(C\) is traversed in the counterclockwise direction. Using Green's theorem, \[\oint_C (P\,dx+Q\,dy) = \iint_R \left( \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y} \right)dA\] Here, \[P=-y, \qquad Q=x\] Therefore, \[\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}=1, \qquad \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=-1\] Hence, \[\oint_C (x\,dy-y\,dx) = \iint_R (1-(-1))\,dA\] \[= 2\iint_R dA = 2(\text{Area of }R)\] The region \(R\) consists of a rectangle of dimensions \(2\times 3\), a semicircle of radius \(1\).
Area of rectangle: \[=2\times 3=6\] Area of semicircle: \[=\frac{1}{2}\pi(1)^2 = \frac{\pi}{2}\] Total area= \(6+\frac{\pi}{2}\) Therefore, \[\oint_C (x\,dy-y\,dx) = 2\left(6+\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\] \[= 12+\pi\] \[\boxed{\text{(c) $12+\pi$}}\]

questions.question: The families of curves represented by the solution of the equation \[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)^n\] for \(n = -1\) and \(n = +1\), respectively, are
questions.explanation:
Given differential equation is \[\frac{dy}{dx} = -\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)^n\] For \(n=-1\), \[\frac{dy}{dx} = -\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)^{-1} = -\frac{y}{x}\] \[\frac{1}{y}dy = -\frac{1}{x}dx\] Integrating, \[\ln y = -\ln x + C\] \[\ln(xy) = C\] \[\Rightarrow\ xy = c \rightarrow\ \text{represents a family of hyperbolas.}\] For \(n=1\), \[\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{x}{y}\] \[y\,dy=-x\,dx\] Integrating, \[\frac{y^2}{2} = -\frac{x^2}{2} + C\] \[\Rightarrow\ x^2 + y^2 = c \rightarrow\ \text{represents a family of circles.}\] Hence, for \(n=-1\) and \(n=1\), the families of curves are hyperbolas and circles, respectively. \[\boxed{\text{(B)}\ \text{Hyperbolas and Circles}}\]
Key points
  • The equation \(xy=c\) represents a rectangular hyperbola.
  • The equation \(x^2+y^2=c\) represents a family of circles centered at the origin.
Mistakes to avoid
  • After integration, simplify the equation into a standard geometric form before identifying the curve.

questions.question: Consider the homogeneous ordinary differential equation \[x^2\,\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} - 3x\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 3y = 0, \qquad x>0\] with \(y(x)\) as a general solution. Given that \(y(1)=1\) and \(y(2)=14\). The value of \(y(1.5)\), rounded off to two decimal places, is
questions.explanation: Given differential equation is \[x^2\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} - 3x\frac{dy}{dx} + 3y = 0\] Assume a solution of the form \[y = x^m\] \[\Rightarrow\ \frac{dy}{dx} = mx^{m-1}\] \[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = m(m-1)x^{m-2}\] Substituting into the differential equation, \[x^2\bigl(m(m-1)x^{m-2}\bigr) - 3x(mx^{m-1}) + 3x^m = 0\] \[\Rightarrow\ \bigl(m(m-1)-3m+3\bigr)x^m = 0\] \[m^2 - 4m + 3 = 0\] \[(m-1)(m-3) = 0\] Hence, the general solution is \(y = c_1x+c_2x^3\) Using the given conditions: \[y(1) = 1 \Rightarrow\ c_1 + c_2 = 1\] \[y(2) = 14 \Rightarrow\ 2c_1 + 8c_2 = 14\] Solving, \(c_1 = -1,\ c_2 = 2\) Therefore, \[y = -x + 2x^3\] At \(x=1.5\), \[y(1.5) = -(1.5) + 2(1.5)^3\] \[= -1.5 + 6.75 = 5.25\] \[\boxed{5.25}\]

questions.question: Which one of the following functions is analytic over the entire complex plane?
questions.explanation:
Examine the analyticity and singularities for each of the given options:
  • \textbf{A.} \(f(z) = \ln(z)\) The complex logarithmic function \(\ln(z) = \ln|z| + j\arg(z)\) is multi-valued. To make it a single-valued analytic function, a branch cut is introduced (typically along the negative real axis from \(0\) to \(-\infty\)). The point \(z = 0\) is a branch point singularity. Therefore, \(\ln(z)\) is not analytic at \(z = 0\) and along its branch cut.
  • \textbf{B.} \(f(z) = e^{1/z}\) Laurent series expansion: \[e^{1/z} = 1 + \frac{1}{z} + \frac{1}{2!z^2} + \frac{1}{3!z^3} + \dots\] Since the principal part (the terms with negative powers of \(z\)) contains infinitely many non-zero terms, \(z = 0\) is an essential singularity. The function is analytic everywhere except at \(z = 0\).
  • \textbf{C.} \(f(z) = \frac{1}{1 - z}\) The function is a rational function. Its singularity occurs where the denominator equals zero: \[1 - z = 0 \Rightarrow z = 1\] Since it is a non-isolated zero of the denominator of order 1, \(z = 1\) is a simple pole. The function is analytic everywhere except at \(z = 1\).
  • \textbf{D.} \(f(z) = \cos(z)\) Taylor series expansion: \[\cos(z) = 1 - \frac{z^2}{2!} + \frac{z^4}{4!} - \frac{z^6}{6!} + \dots\] The series converges for all \(z \in \mathbb{C}\) (\(R = \infty\)). It contains no negative powers of \(z\), meaning it possesses no singularities in the finite complex plane. Thus, \(\cos(z)\) is an entire function (always analytic).
\[\boxed{D. \cos (z)}\]
Key points
  • Classification of Singularities:
    • Pole: If the principal part of the Laurent series has a finite number of terms.
    • Essential Singularity: If the principal part has infinitely many terms (e.g., \(e^{1/z}\) at \(z=0\)).
    • Branch Point: A point where a multi-valued function cannot be defined continuously as a single-valued function (e.g., \(z=0\) for \(\ln z\)).

questions.question: If \(X\) and \(Y\) are random variables such that \(E[2X + Y] = 0\) and \(E[X + 2Y] = 33\), then \(E[X] + E[Y] =\\).
questions.explanation: Given: \[E(2X + Y) = 0\ \text{and}\ E(X + 2Y) = 33\] Using the linearity property of expectation, \[E(aX + bY) = aE(X) + bE(Y)\] \[2E(X) + E(Y) = 0 \tag{1}\] \[E(X) + 2E(Y) = 33 \tag{2}\] Adding equations \((1)\) and \((2)\), \[3E(X) + 3E(Y) = 33 \Rightarrow\ 3\big(E(X) + E(Y)\big) = 33\] \[E(X) + E(Y) = 11\] \[\boxed{11}\]

questions.question:
Let \(Z\) be an exponential random variable with mean 1. That is, the cumulative distribution function of \(Z\) is given by \[F_Z(x) = \begin{cases}
        1 - e^{-x}& if\ x \geq 0\\
        0& if\ x < 0
    \end{cases}\] Then \(Pr(Z > 2|Z > 1)\), rounded off to two decimal places, is equal to .
questions.explanation:
The cumulative distribution function of the exponential random variable \(Z\) is \[F_Z(x)=
\begin{cases}
1-e^{-x}, & x\geq 0 \\
0, & x<0
\end{cases}\] Hence, the probability density function is \[f_Z(x)=e^{-x}, \qquad x\geq 0\] We need to evaluate \(P(Z>2 \mid Z>1)\) Since \(Z>2\) automatically implies \(Z>1\), \[P(Z>2 \mid Z>1) = \frac{P(Z>2)}{P(Z>1)}\] Now, \[P(Z > a) = \int_a^\infty e^{-z}\,dz\] Therefore, \[P(Z > 2) = \int_2^\infty e^{-z}\,dz = \left[-e^{-z}\right]_2^\infty = e^{-2}\] Similarly, \[P(Z > 1) = \int_1^\infty e^{-z}\,dz = \left[-e^{-z}\right]_1^\infty = e^{-1}\] Hence, \[P(Z > 2 \mid Z > 1) = \frac{e^{-2}}{e^{-1}} = e^{-1} \approx 0.3679\] Rounded to two decimal places, \[0.37\] \[\boxed{0.37}\]

questions.question: The RC circuit shown below has a variable resistance \(R(t)\) given by the following expression: \[R(t) = R_0 \left(1 - \frac{t}{T}\right) \quad \text{for } 0 \le t < T\] where \(R_0 = 1\ \Omega\), and \(C = 1\text{ F}\). We are also given that \(T = 3\ R_0C\) and the source voltage is \(V_s = 1\text{ V}\). If the current at time \(t = 0\) is \(1\text{ A}\). Then the current \(I(t)\), in amperes, at time \(t = T/2\) is . (Rounded off to 2 decimal places).
questions.explanation: Applying KCL, \[C\frac{dv(t)}{dt} + \frac{v(t)-V_s}{R(t)} = 0, \qquad \text{where v(t) is the voltage across capacitor}\] Since, \(\qquad \qquad \qquad C=1, \qquad V_s=1, \qquad R(t)=R_0\left(1-\dfrac{t}{T}\right)\) \[\text{and, } T=3R_0C=3~\text{s},\] the differential equation becomes \[\frac{dv(t)}{dt} + \frac{v(t)-1}{1-\dfrac{t}{3}} = 0\] \[\Rightarrow \frac{dv(t)}{v(t)-1} = -\frac{dt}{1-\dfrac{t}{3}}\] Integrating both sides, \[\ln(v(t)-1) = 3\ln(t-3)+\ln K, \qquad \text{where \(K\) is a constant.}\] Hence, \[\ln\!\left(\frac{v(t)-1}{(t-3)^3}\right) = \ln K\] Taking antilog, \[v(t)=1+K(t-3)^3\] The capacitor current is \[i(t) = C\frac{dv(t)}{dt} = \frac{dv(t)}{dt} = 3K(t-3)^2\] Using the initial condition, \(i(0)=1~\text{A},\) we get \[1 = 3K(0-3)^2 = 27K\] \[\Rightarrow K=\frac{1}{27}\] At \(t=\dfrac{T}{2} = \dfrac{3}{2} = 1.5~\text{s},\) the current is \[i\!\left(\frac{T}{2}\right) = 3\left(\frac{1}{27}\right)(1.5)^2\] \[= \frac{3}{27}\times\frac{15}{10}\times\frac{15}{10} = \frac14 = 0.25~\text{A}\] Hence, \[\boxed{0.25}\]

questions.ref: Network Theorems For DC & Miscellaneous Topics Q1
questions.question: Consider the two-port resistive network shown in the figure. When an excitation of \(5\text{ V}\) is applied across Port 1, and Port 2 is shorted, the current through the short circuit at Port 2 is measured to be \(1\text{ A}\) (see (a) in the figure). Now, if an excitation of \(5\text{ V}\) is applied across Port 2, and Port 1 is shorted (see (b) in the figure), what is the current through the short circuit at Port 1?
questions.explanation: A passive linear bilateral network satisfies the Reciprocity Theorem. It states that if a voltage source \(V_1\) applied at one port produces a current \(I_1\) at another port, then interchanging the position of the excitation and the response gives \[\frac{V_1}{I_1} = \frac{V_2}{I_2}\] From the given circuit in question, \[V_1=5~\text{V}, \qquad I_1=1~\text{A}\] Applying the Reciprocity Theorem, \[\frac{V_1}{I_1} = \frac{V_2}{I_2} \ \Rightarrow \ \frac{5}{1} = \frac{5}{I_2}\] \[\] \[I_2 = 1~\text{A}\] Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{B. }1~\text{A}}\]

questions.subject: network-theory
questions.question: In the circuit shown, if \(v(t)=2sin(1000t)\) volts, \(R=1~k\,\Omega\) and \(C=1~\mu\text{F}\), then the steady-state current \(i(t)\), in milliamperes (mA), is
questions.explanation:
To solve the problem we can first convert the capacitors arranged in a Y to that in \(\Delta\). When arranged in \(\Delta\), the capacitors would be of value C/3 (C being the original value). Hence we have a \(\Delta\)-connected load, whose each arm consists of a resistance R and capacitance C/3 in parallel. Let each arm impedance be Z. \[Z = R||(3)/j\omega C\] Here \(\omega = 1000\,\text{rad/s}\), \(R=1~k\,\Omega\) and \(C=1~\mu\text{F}\) \[\therefore Z = 900 - j300 \Omega\] The impedance seen by the voltage source would \(Z_{eq}=Z||2Z=600-j200\Omega\) The voltage in phasor form is \(V=2\angle0^{\circ}\) \[\therefore I = \frac{2\angle0^{\circ}}{600-j200} = 0.003+j0.001\,\text{A}=3+j1\,\text{mA}\]. The time domain equation would be \(i(t)=3 sin (1000t)+cos(1000t) \,\text{mA}\).
Key points
  • The same problem can be solved by converting the load to an equivalent Y form, but the approach of converting to \(\Delta\) form is more convenient and simple. Hence the other approach is not recommended.
Mistakes to avoid
  • When converting a network from Y to \(\Delta\) the arm impedances get multiplied by 3. However since capacitive impedance is inversely proportional to the capacitance value, the capacitance needs to be divided by 3.
\[\boxed{(c) 3sin(1000t)+cos(1000t)}\]

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: Consider the signal \(\displaystyle f(t) = 1 + 2 \cos(\pi t) + 3 \sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}t\right) + 4 \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}t + \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\), where \(t\) is in seconds. Its fundamental time period, in seconds, is .
questions.explanation:
Given the continuous-time signal: \[f(t) = 1 + 2 \cos(\pi t) + 3 \sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}t\right) + 4 \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}t + \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\] The individual radian frequencies of the sinusoidal components are: \[\omega_1 = \pi\] \[\omega_2 = \frac{2\pi}{3}\] \[\omega_3 = \frac{\pi}{2}\] The fundamental frequency \(\omega_0\) is the Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) of the individual frequencies: \[\omega_0 = \text{GCD}\left(\pi, \frac{2\pi}{3}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right) = \frac{\pi}{6}\] The fundamental period is: \[N = \frac{2\pi}{\omega_0} = \frac{2\pi}{(\pi/6)} = 12\] \[\boxed{12}\]
Key points
  • For a signal \(x(t) = x_1(t) + x_2(t) + \dots + x_n(t)\), the fundamental frequency is \(\omega_0 = \text{GCD}(\omega_1, \omega_2, \dots, \omega_n)\).
  • To find the GCD of fractions: \(\text{GCD}\left(\frac{a}{b}, \frac{c}{d}\right) = \frac{\text{GCD}(a, c)}{\text{LCM}(b, d)}\).
  • Alternatively, the fundamental period \(T_0\) can be found by taking the Least Common Multiple (LCM) of the individual periods: \(T_0 = \text{LCM}(T_1, T_2, \dots, T_n)\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Calculating the LCM of the frequencies instead of the GCD. Remember: Fundamental Period \(\rightarrow\) LCM, Fundamental Frequency \(\rightarrow\) GCD.
  • Getting confused by the constant term (\(1\)). A constant term is a DC signal (\(\omega = 0\)) and does not dictate the fundamental period of the varying components.

questions.question: Let \(H(z)\) be the \(z\)-transform of a real-valued discrete-time signal \(h[n]\). If \(P(z) = H(z)H\left(\frac{1}{z}\right)\) has a zero at \(z = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}j\), and \(P(z)\) has a total of four zeros, which one of the following plots represents all the zeros correctly?
questions.explanation:
\[P(Z) = H(Z)H\left(\frac{1}{Z}\right)\] (i) \(h(n)\) is real. So \(p(n)\) will be also real (ii) \(P(z) = P(z^{-1})\) From (i) : if \(z_1\) is a zero of \(P(z)\), then \(z_1^*\) will be also a zero of \(P(z)\). From (ii): If \(z_1\) is a zero of \(P(z)\), then \(\frac{1}{z_1}\) will be also a zero of \(P(z)\). So, the 4 zeros are, \[z_1 = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}j\] \[z_2 = z_1^* = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2}j\] \[z_3 = \frac{1}{z_1} = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}j} = 1 - j\] \[z_4 = \left(\frac{1}{z_1}\right)^* = z_3^* = 1 + j\] \[\boxed{\text{D}}\]
Key points
  • If a discrete-time signal \(h[n]\) is real-valued, its zeros and poles in the \(z\)-domain occur in complex conjugate pairs.
  • For a filter with transfer function \(P(z) = H(z)H(z^{-1})\), the zeros and poles also exhibit reciprocal symmetry (if \(z_0\) is a root, so is \(1/z_0\)).
  • Combining both properties, complex roots appear in quartets: \(z_0\), \(z_0^*\), \(1/z_0\), and \(1/z_0^*\).

questions.question: In an ideal \(pn\) junction with an ideality factor of \(1\) at \(T=300\ K\), the magnitude of the reverse-bias voltage required to reach \(75\%\) of its reverse saturation current, rounded off to \(2\) decimal places, is _____ \(mV\). [\(k = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\ JK^{-1}\), \(h = 6.625 \times 10^{-34}\ Js\), \(q = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\ C\)]
questions.explanation:
The thermal voltage \(V_{T}\) at a temperature \(T = 300\,\text{K}\) is calculated using the Boltzmann constant \(k\) and the electron charge \(q\): \[V_{T} = \frac{kT}{q} = \frac{1.38 \times 10^{-23} \times 300}{1.602 \times 10^{-19}}\,\text{V} = 25.843\,\text{mV}\] The diode current \(I\) is given by the standard diode equation. For a reverse bias condition where the current is \(-75\%\) of the reverse saturation current \(I_{0}\): \[I = I_{0} \left( e^{V/V_{T}} - 1 \right) = -\frac{3}{4} I_{0}\] Simplifying the equation to solve for the voltage \(V\): \[e^{V/V_{T}} - 1 = -0.75\] \[e^{V/V_{T}} = 0.25\] \[V = V_{T} \ln(0.25) = 25.843\,\text{mV} \times (-1.386) = -35.83\,\text{mV}\] The magnitude of the reverse bias potential \(V_{R}\) is: \[V_{R} = |V| = 35.83\,\text{mV}\] \[\boxed{35.83}\]
Key points
  • In reverse bias, \(V\) is negative, resulting in a current \(I\) that approaches \(-I_{0}\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • The question asks for the magnitude of the reverse bias; the final answer should be positive.

questions.question: The figure shows the high-frequency C-V curve of a MOS capacitor (at \(\text{T} = 300\text{ K}\)) with \(\Phi_{ms} = 0\text{ V}\) and no oxide charges. The flat-band, inversion, and accumulation conditions are represented, respectively, by the points [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
From the graph, the capacitance is maximum at large negative gate voltage (point P). This indicates accumulation occurs for negative gate bias, which is possible only for a p-type substrate because holes (majority carriers) accumulate at the oxide-semiconductor interface. As the gate voltage becomes positive, holes are repelled from the interface, leading to depletion (point Q), and for sufficiently large positive gate voltage, inversion occurs (point R). In a high-frequency C-V measurement, the inversion carriers cannot follow the AC signal, so the capacitance remains at its minimum value. Therefore, the shape of the graph itself indicates that the MOS capacitor is an NMOS capacitor fabricated on a p-type substrate. Analysing each labelled point on the high-frequency C--V curve of the MOS capacitor: At \(P\) (large negative \(V_G\)) --- Accumulation: Holes accumulate at the oxide--semiconductor interface, so capacitance is maximum (\(\approx C_{ox}\)). At \(Q\) (\(V_G = 0\)) --- Flat-band: Since \(\Phi_{ms} = 0\) and there is no oxide charge, flat-band occurs exactly at zero gate voltage. Between \(Q\) and \(R\) (positive \(V_G\)) --- Depletion: Holes are repelled from the interface, creating a depletion region; capacitance decreases as the depletion width widens. At \(R\) (large positive \(V_G\)) --- Inversion: Minority electrons form an inversion layer. In the high-frequency C--V measurement, inversion charge cannot follow the AC signal, so capacitance stays at its minimum value \(C_{min}\). The correct identification of the sequence flat-band \(\to\) inversion \(\to\) accumulation on the curve is: \[\boxed{(B)\,Q,\, R,\, P}\]
Key points
  • In a p-type MOS capacitor: accumulation (\(V_G \ll 0\)) gives \(C \approx C_{ox}\); depletion (\(0 < V_G < V_T\)) reduces \(C\); inversion (\(V_G > V_T\)) gives \(C_{min}\).
  • At high frequency, the inversion layer charge cannot respond to the AC signal, so \(C\) does not recover and remains at \(C_{min}\) --- unlike low-frequency C--V where \(C\) rises back to \(C_{ox}\).
  • The total MOS capacitance in depletion is \(C = C_{ox}C_{dep}/(C_{ox} + C_{dep})\), which decreases as depletion width \(W_d\) increases.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not apply low-frequency C--V behaviour (where \(C\) recovers at inversion) to a high-frequency measurement --- at high frequency \(C\) stays at \(C_{min}\) in inversion.
  • Do not assume flat-band always occurs at \(V_G = 0\); it only does so when both \(\phi_{ms} = 0\) and \(Q_{ox} = 0\).
  • For a p-type substrate, inversion occurs at positive \(V_G\), not negative --- confusing substrate type reverses the entire C--V curve.

If the absorption coefficient of Germanium at 600 nm is \(3 \times 10^4 cm^{-1}\) and the bandgap is 0.66 eV, the thickness of the Germanium layer, rounded off to 3 decimal places, is ____ \(\mu m\).

questions.question: The quantum efficiency (\(\eta\)) and responsivity (\(R\)) at a wavelength \(\lambda\) (in \(\mu m\)) in a p-i-n photodetector are related by
questions.explanation:
The quantum efficiency \(\eta\) of a photodetector relates the output current to input optical power by: \[\eta = \frac{I_{out}}{q} \times \frac{hf}{P_{in}}\] The responsivity \(R\) is defined as: \[R = \frac{I_{out}}{P_{in}}\] Expressing \(R\) in terms of \(\eta\): \[R = \eta \times \frac{q}{hf} = \eta \times \frac{q\lambda}{hc}\] If \(\lambda\) is given in \(\mu\text{m}\), substituting \(\lambda\) in \(\mu\text{m}\): \[R = \eta\lambda \times \frac{q \times 10^{-6}}{hc}\] Using the standard constant \(hc/(q \times 10^{-6}) \approx 1.24\,\text{W}/(\text{A}\cdot\mu\text{m})\): \[\boxed{(A) \, R = \frac{\eta\lambda}{1.24}}\]
Key points
  • Responsivity \(R = I_{out}/P_{in}\) in A/W measures how efficiently a photodetector converts optical power to electrical current.
  • The relation \(R = \eta\lambda/1.24\) (with \(\lambda\) in \(\mu\text{m}\)) is a standard and widely used result; the constant \(1.24\) arises from \(hc/q \approx 1.24\,\text{eV}\cdot\mu\text{m}\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse quantum efficiency \(\eta\) (dimensionless, \(0 \leq \eta \leq 1\)) with responsivity \(R\) (in A/W); \(\eta\) is the fraction of photons converted to electron-hole pairs, while \(R\) accounts for the energy per photon.
  • Ensure \(\lambda\) is in \(\mu\text{m}\) when using \(R = \eta\lambda/1.24\); using \(\lambda\) in nm gives a result \(10^3\) times too small.

questions.question: In the circuit shown, \(V_s\) is a square wave of period \(T\) with maximum and minimum values of \(8\text{ V}\) and \(-10\text{ V}\), respectively. Assume that the diode is ideal and \(R_1 = R_2 = 50\,\Omega\). The average value of \(V_L\) is volts (rounded off to 1 decimal place).
questions.explanation:
Case 1: For \(0 < t < T/2\), \(V_s = 8\,\text{V}\). So, diode will be off and can be replaced with open circuit \[\therefore \quad V_L = \left[ \frac{50}{50 + 50} \right] \times 8 = 4\,\text{V} \quad \text{[by Voltage Division Rule]}\] Case 2:For \(T/2 < t < T\), \(V_s = -10\,\text{V}\). So, diode will be ON and hence it will be short circuited and \(R_1\) can be neglected as it comes across short circuit. \[\therefore V_L = -10\,\text{V}\] Therefore, equivalent output waveform will be Average value of \(V_L(t)\) is given as \[V_{av} = \frac{1}{T} \int_{0}^{T} v_L(t) dt\] \[V_{L_{av}} = \frac{1}{T} \left[ \int_{0}^{T/2} 4 \cdot dt + \int_{T/2}^{T} (-10) dt \right]\] \[V_{L_{av}} = \frac{1}{T} \left[ 4 \times \frac{T}{2} - 10 \times \frac{T}{2} \right]\] \[V_{L_{av}} = \frac{1}{T} \times (-6) \times \frac{T}{2} = -3\,\text{V}\] (OR) \[V_{av} = \frac{\text{Area of one period of wave from}}{\text{Time period}}\] \[V_{av} = \frac{\left(4 \times \frac{T}{2} - 10 \times \frac{T}{2}\right)}{T}\] \[V_{av} = \frac{\frac{T}{2}(4-10)}{T} = \frac{-6}{2} = -3\,\text{V}\] \[\boxed{\text{ The average value of } V_L \text{ is } -3\,\text{V}.}\]
Key points
  • Analyze the diode state by finding out voltages at both terminals.
  • When the diode is forward-biased (ON) and ideal, it acts as a short circuit, bypassing any parallel resistor.

questions.question: In the circuit shown, the breakdown voltage and the maximum current of the Zener diode are \(20\text{ V}\) and \(60\text{ mA}\), respectively. The values of \(R_1\) and \(R_L\) are \(200\,\Omega\) and \(1\,\text{k}\Omega\), respectively. What is the range of \(V_i\) that will maintain the Zener diode in the 'on' state?
questions.explanation:
Given, \[V_z = 20\,\text{V}\] \[I_{z\max} = 60\,\text{mA}\] Case 1: Finding Lower limit of \(V_i\) Initially for lower values of \(V_i\) zener diode is OFF, so by applying Open Circuit Test, \[V_o = \frac{V_i \times 1\text{k}}{0.2\text{k} + 1\text{k}} = \frac{V_i}{1.2}\] Zener diode will be ON i.e. it goes into breakdown, when \(V_L > V_z\) or \(V_0 > V_z\) \[\frac{V_i}{1.2} > 20\,\text{V}\] \[\boxed{V_i > 24\,\text{V}}\] So \(V_i\) should be atleast 24V so that zener is maintained in ON state. Case 2: Finding upper limit of \(V_i\) When Zener diode is in breakdown region, \[I_1 = \frac{V_i - 20}{0.2\,\text{k}\Omega} = \frac{V_i - 20}{0.2}\,\text{mA}\] \[I_L = \frac{V_o}{R_L} = \frac{20}{1\,\text{k}\Omega} = 20\,\text{mA}\] \[I_z = I_1 - I_L = \frac{V_i - 20}{0.2} - 20\] For safe operation, \(I_z \leq I_{z\max}\), as if \(I_z > I_{z\max}\) then zener will be damaged and no longer be considered ON \[\frac{V_i - 20}{0.2} - 20 \leq 60\] \[\boxed{ V_i \leq 36\,\text{V} }\] When \(V_i\) is at maximum value and load current is minimum(\(I_{L\min}\)) then zener current is maximum(\(I_{Z\max}\)) \[I_{L\min} = \frac{20}{1\text{k}} = 20\text{mA}\] \[\frac{V_i - 20}{200} \leq I_{Z\max} + I_{L\min}\] \[\frac{V_i - 20}{200} \leq 80\,\text{mA}\] \[\frac{V_i - 20}{200} \leq \frac{80}{1000}\] \[V_i - 20 \leq 16\] \[\boxed{V_i \leq 36\text{ V}}\] Hence, \[\boxed{\text{(B)}\quad24 < V_i < 36\,\text{V}}\]
Key points
  • It is a voltage regulator because if there is a fluctuation in the load or input voltage , those are absorbed by zener as current.
  • The minimum input voltage (\(V_{i(\text{min})}\)) required to turn the Zener diode ON is found by assuming the diode is open and calculating the voltage across it using the voltage divider rule.
  • The maximum input voltage (\(V_{i(\text{max})}\)) is determined by the maximum current rating of the Zener diode (\(I_{z\max}\)).

questions.question: In the circuits shown, the threshold voltage of each nMOS transistor is \(0.6\,\text{V}\). Ignoring the effect of channel length modulation and body bias, the values of \(V_{out1}\) and \(V_{out2}\), respectively, in volts, are

Method 1
Given, threshold voltage of each NMOS transistor is \(0.6\,\text{V}\) and \(V_G = 3\,\text{V} \text{ for all NMOS transistors}\).
Method 2
Given circuit (I) is shown in below figure and the n-MOS used have threshold voltage as \(0.6\,\text{V}\). For pass transistor logic \(V_{GS}\) is maintained as \(V_{TH}\).
In a pass transistor logic, \(V_{GS}\) is automatically maintained at \(V_{TH}\). If \(V_G\) is fixed, \(V_S\) should be adjusted so that \[V_G - V_S = V_{TH} \implies V_S = V_G - V_{TH}\] From above figure, \[V_{s_1} = V_{G_1} - V_{TH} = 3 - 0.6 = 2.4\,\text{V}\] \[V_{s_2} = V_{G_2} - V_{TH} = 2.4 - 0.6 = 1.8\,\text{V} = V_{out1}\] \[\text{Here, }V_{s_1} = V_{G_1} - V_{TH} = 3 - 0.6 = 2.4\,\text{V}\] \[V_{s_2} = V_{G_2} - V_{TH} = 3 - 0.6 = 2.4\,\text{V}\] \[V_{s_3} = V_{G_3} - V_{TH} = 3 - 0.6 = 2.4\,\text{V} = V_{out2}\] Applying KVL in loop (1), we get \[-3 + V_{GS} + V_{GS} + V_{out_1} = 0\] \[V_{out_1} = 3 - 2V_{GS} = 3 - 2 \times 0.6\] \[V_{out_1} = 1.8\,\text{V}\] Similarly from circuit (II), Applying kVL in loop (1) \[-3 + V_{GS} + V_{out_2} = 0\] \[V_{out_2} = 3 - V_{GS} = 3 - 0.6\] \[V_{out_2} = 2.4\,\text{volt}\] \[\boxed{\text{(C)}\quad 1.8\ \text{and}\ 2.4}\]

questions.question: In the circuit shown, the threshold voltages of the pMOS (\(|V_{tp}|\)) and nMOS (\(V_{tn}\)) transistors are both equal to \(1\,\text{V}\). All the transistors have the same output resistance \(r_{ds}\) of \(6\,\text{M}\Omega\). The other parameters are listed below: \(\mu_n C_{\text{ox}} = 60\,\mu\text{A/V}^2 ; \left(W/L\right)_{\text{nMOS}} = 5\) \(\mu_p C_{\text{ox}} = 30\,\mu\text{A/V}^2 ; \left(W/L\right)_{\text{pMOS}} = 10\) \(\mu_n\) and \(\mu_p\) are the carrier mobilities, and \(C_{\text{ox}}\) is the oxide capacitance per unit area. Ignoring the effect of channel length modulation and body bias, the gain of the circuit is _________ (rounded off to \(1\) decimal place).
questions.explanation:
Given, \(\text{For N-MOS,\quad } \mu_n C_{ox} = 60\,\mu\text{A/V}^2 \quad W/L = 5\) \(\text{For P-MOS,\quad} \mu_p C_{ox} = 30\,\mu\text{A/V}^2 \quad W/L = 10\) Output resistance, \(r_{ds} = 6\,\text{M}\Omega\) For both MOSFET, \(|V_t| = 1\,\text{V}\) From above figure, the \(M_3\) and \(M_4\) have same \(V_{SG}\) so \(V_{SG} = V_{DD}/2 = 4/2 = 2\,\text{V}\) and \[I_D = \frac{\mu_n C_{ox}}{2} \frac{W}{L} \left[V_{GS} - |V_t|\right]^2\] \[I_D = \frac{\mu_p C_{ox}}{2} \frac{W}{L} \left[V_{GS} - |V_t|\right]^2\] \[I_D = \frac{1}{2} \times 30 \times 10 \times (2 - 1)^2\] \[I_D = 150\,\mu\text{A}\] \[g_{mn} = \sqrt{2 I_D \cdot \left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_n \cdot \mu_n C_{ox}}\] \[g_{mn} = \sqrt{2 \times 150 \times 5 \times 60}\] \[g_{mn} = 300\,\mu\text{A/V}\] Here \(M_2\),\(M_3\),\(M_4\) form active load for \(M_1\) and the resistance seen through the drain of \(M_1\) looking up is \(r_{ds}\) of \(M_2\). So the AC small signal equivalent is given by, \[\text{Gain} = \frac{V_0}{V_{in}}\] \[V_0 = -g_{mn} V_{in} [r_{ds} || r_{ds}]\] \[V_0 = \frac{-g_{mn} V_{in} r_{ds}}{2} =\frac{-300 \times 10^{-6} \times 6 \times 10^6}{2}\] \[\therefore \quad \text{Gain} = \frac{-g_{mn} V_{in} r_{ds}}{2 V_{in}}\] \[\boxed{ \text{Gain} = -900 }\]
Key points
  • In the biasing branch, two identical diode-connected PMOS transistors in series divide the supply voltage equally, establishing \(V_{SG} = \frac{V_{DD}}{2}\).
  • The drain current \(I_D\) is determined by this \(V_{SG}\) and is mirrored to the active load PMOS.
  • The transconductance of the amplifying NMOS is calculated using \(g_{mn} = \sqrt{2 I_D \mu_n C_{ox} (W/L)_n}\).
  • The voltage gain of a common-source amplifier with an active load is given by \(-g_{mn} (r_{ds\_n} || r_{ds\_p})\).

So, we get \(I_{D_3} = I_{D_4} = 0\,\text{A}\) Which gives, \(I_{D_2} = I_{D_6}\) \(T_5\) and \(T_6\) are in series and \(T_7\) and \(T_5\) form another current mirror, therefore we get, \[I_{D_5} = I_{D_6} = I_{D_2} \quad \dots\text{(ii)}\] \[\frac{I_{D_7}}{I_{D_5}} = \frac{\left(\dfrac{W}{L}\right)_7}{\left(\dfrac{W}{L}\right)_5}\] \[I_{out} = I_{D_7} = I_{D_5} \left[ \frac{\left(\dfrac{W}{L}\right)_7}{\left(\dfrac{W}{L}\right)_5} \right] = I_{D_5} \left( \frac{40}{10} \right)\] \[I_{out} = 4 I_{D_5} = 4 I_{D_2} \quad [\text{From equation (ii)}]\] \[I_{out} = 4 \times 1.5\,\text{mA} \quad [\text{From equation (i)}]\] \[\boxed{ I_{out} = 6\,\text{mA}}\]

questions.question: Consider a long-channel MOSFET with a channel length \(1\,\mu\text{m}\) and width \(10\,\mu\text{m}\). The device parameters are acceptor concentration \(N_A = 5 \times 10^{16}\,\text{cm}^{-3}\), electron mobility \(\mu_n = 800\,\text{cm}^2\text{/V-s}\), oxide capacitance/area \(C_{ox} = 3.45 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{F/cm}^2\), threshold voltage \(V_T = 0.7\,\text{V}\). The drain saturation current (\(I_{Dsat}\)) for a gate voltage of \(5\,\text{V}\) is _________ mA (rounded off to two decimal places). \([\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-14}\,\text{F/cm}, \varepsilon_{Si} = 11.9]\)

questions.question: A CMOS inverter, designed to have a mid-point voltage \(V_I\) equal to half of \(V_{dd}\), as shown in the figure, has the following parameters: \[V_{dd} = 3\text{ V}\] \[\mu_nC_{ox} = 100\text{ }\mu\text{A/V}^2 \text{ ; } V_{tn} = 0.7\text{ V for nMOS}\] \[\mu_pC_{ox} = 40\text{ }\mu\text{A/V}^2 \text{ ; } |V_{tp}| = 0.9\text{ V for pMOS}\] The ratio of \(\left(W/L\right)_n\) to \(\left(W/L\right)_p\) is equal to _________ (rounded off to 3 decimal places).

Given, \[V_{dd} = 3\text{ V}\] \[\mu_nC_{ox} = 100\text{ }\mu\text{A/V}^2 \text{ ; } V_{tn} = 0.7\text{ V for nMOS}\] \[\mu_pC_{ox} = 40\text{ }\mu\text{A/V}^2 \text{ ; } |V_{tp}| = 0.9\text{ V for pMOS}\] From the graph \(V_{in} = V_{DD}/2 \text{ and } V_{out} = V_{DD}/2\) The CMOS inverter circuit is given below where, \[I_{Dp} = I_{Dn} \text{ and } V_{SGp} = V_{GSn} = 1.5\] and both MOSFETs are in saturation. \[\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} (\mu_n C_{ox}) \left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_n [V_{GSN} - V_{TN}]^2 = \frac{1}{2} (\mu_p C_{ox}) \left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_p [V_{SGP} + V_{TP}]^2\] \[100 \times 10^{-6} \left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_n [1.5 - 0.7]^2 = 40 \times 10^{-6} \left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_p [1.5 - 0.9]^2\] \[\Rightarrow \frac{\left(\dfrac{W}{L}\right)_n}{\left(\dfrac{W}{L}\right)_p} = \frac{40}{100} \times \frac{(0.6)^2}{(0.8)^2} = 0.225\]

questions.question: In the circuit shown, the clock frequency, i.e., the frequency of the Clk signal, is \(12\,\text{kHz}\). The frequency of the signal at \(Q_2\) is kHz.
questions.explanation:
From the given circuit diagram, the input expressions for the flip-flops can be written as: \[D_1 = \overline{Q}_1 \cdot \overline{Q}_2\] \[D_2 = Q_1\] Let us trace the state transitions starting from an initial state \((Q_1Q_2) = (00)\):
Clock Pulse\(Q_1\)\(Q_2\)\(D_1 = \overline{Q}_1 \cdot \overline{Q}_2\)\(D_2 = Q_1\)
Initially\(0\)\(0\)\(1\)\(0\)
\(1^{\text{st}}\)\(1\)\(0\)\(0\)\(1\)
\(2^{\text{nd}}\)\(0\)\(1\)\(0\)\(0\)
\(3^{\text{rd}}\)\(0\)\(0\)\(1\)\(0\)
The sequence of states repeats after every \(3\) clock cycles: \[(00) \rightarrow (10) \rightarrow (01) \rightarrow (00)\] Since the counter has a cycle length of \(3\), the modulus of the counter is \(N = 3\). The frequency of the output signal at \(Q_2\) is given by dividing the input clock frequency by the modulus of the counter: \[f_{Q2} = \frac{f_{\text{clk}}}{N} = \frac{12\,\text{kHz}}{3} = 4\,\text{kHz}\] \[\boxed{4}\]
Key points
  • The modulus (\(N\)) of a synchronous counter is the number of unique states visited before the sequence repeats.
  • The output frequency from any flip-flop stage of a periodic counter is \(f_{\text{out}} = \frac{f_{\text{clk}}}{N}\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume the modulus is always \(2^n\) (\(4\) for two flip-flops); trace the state table explicitly to find the actual repeating sequence.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.ref: Logic Families and Semiconductor Memories Q1
questions.question: In the circuit shown, what are the values of \(F\) for \(EN = 0\) and \(EN = 1\), respectively?
questions.explanation:
The circuit shows a tri-state logic buffer with an active-high enable line (\(\text{EN}\)) controlling a PMOS and NMOS output stage. We evaluate the circuit behavior for both cases: Case 1: When \(\text{EN} = 0\)
  • Output of the upper NAND gate \(= \overline{0 \cdot \text{D}} = 1\). This high voltage turns OFF the PMOS transistor.
  • Input to the inverter \(= 0 \implies\) output of the inverter \(= 1\).
  • Output of the lower NOR gate \(= \overline{1 + \text{D}} = 0\). This low voltage turns OFF the NMOS transistor.
Since both transistors are completely cut off, the output terminal \(\text{F}\) is disconnected from both \(\text{V}_{\text{dd}}\) and ground, resulting in an unknown high-impedance state: \[\text{F} = \text{Hi-Z}\] Case 2: When \(\text{EN} = 1\)
  • Output of the upper NAND gate \(= \overline{1 \cdot \text{D}} = \overline{\text{D}}\).
  • Input to the inverter \(= 1 \implies\) output of the inverter \(= 0\).
  • Output of the lower NOR gate \(= \overline{0 + \text{D}} = \overline{\text{D}}\).
Now, the signal driving both gates is \(\overline{\text{D}}\):
  • If \(\text{D} = 0\), the gate drive is \(1 \implies\) PMOS is OFF, NMOS is ON \(\implies \text{F} = 0\).
  • If \(\text{D} = 1\), the gate drive is \(0 \implies\) PMOS is ON, NMOS is OFF \(\implies \text{F} = 1\).
Thus, the output tracks the input directly: \[\text{F} = \text{D}\] Therefore, the values of \(\text{F}\) are \(\text{Hi-Z}\) and \(\text{D}\), respectively. \[\boxed{\text{(B) Hi-Z and D}}\]
Key points
  • A PMOS transistor conducts when its gate is driven low (\(0\)), whereas an NMOS transistor conducts when its gate is driven high (\(1\)).
  • When both the pull-up and pull-down networks are turned off simultaneously, the output terminal enters the high-impedance (\(\text{Hi-Z}\)) state.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume the output is fixed at logic \(0\) when \(\text{EN}=0\); a disconnected node cannot pull the output to ground.

questions.question: In the circuit shown, \(A\) and \(B\) are the inputs and \(F\) is the output. What is the functionality of the circuit?
questions.explanation:
The circuit operation is analyzed for all input combinations of \(A\) and \(B\):
Method 1
From the above logic transitions, the truth table is:
\(\mathbf{A}\)\(\mathbf{B}\)\(\mathbf{P_1}\)\(\mathbf{P_2}\)\(\mathbf{N_1}\)\(\mathbf{N_2}\)\(\mathbf{F}\)

01OFFONONOFF0

The output expression corresponds to an XNOR gate: \[F = \overline{A}\,\overline{B} + AB = A \text{ XNOR } B\]
Method 2
Analysing the NMOS side, At \(A = 1\), \[N_2 \text{ will be ON} \implies F = B \implies F = AB\] At \(B = 1\), \[N_1 \text{ will be ON} \implies F = A \implies F = AB\] Now analysing the PMOS side, At \(A = 0\),\(B = 0\) \[P_1 \text{and } P_2 \text{ both} \text{ will be ON thus F=} V_{DD} \text{(HIGH)} \implies F =\overline{A}\,\overline{B}\] Combining both, \[F = AB+\overline{A}\,\overline{B}\]
\[\boxed{(B)XNOR}\]
Key points
  • PMOS transistors conduct with a low input voltage, while NMOS transistors conduct with a high input voltage.
  • The lower pass-transistors pass the input variables directly to the output node when conducting.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume the NMOS sources are tied to ground; they are connected to input nodes \(A\) and \(B\).

questions.question: The block diagram of a system is illustrated in the figure shown, where \(X(s)\) is the input and \(Y(s)\) is the output. The transfer function \(H(s) = \dfrac{Y(s)}{X(s)}\) is
questions.explanation:
Method 1
Using block diagram reduction: The overall transfer function \(H(s)\) with the final feedback path: \[H(s) = \frac{\frac{s^2 + 1}{s(s^2 + s + 1)}}{1 + \frac{s^2 + 1}{s(s^2 + s + 1)}} = \frac{s^2 + 1}{s^3 + 2s^2 + s + 1}\]
Method 2
Using Mason's Gain Formula: \[T.F = \frac{\sum P_{k}\Delta_{k}}{\Delta} = \frac{(s + \frac{1}{s})(\frac{1}{s})}{1 - [-(s + \frac{1}{s}) - (s + \frac{1}{s})(\frac{1}{s})]} = \frac{\frac{s^2 + 1}{s^2}}{1 + \frac{s^2 + 1}{s} + \frac{s^2 + 1}{s^2}} = \frac{s^2 + 1}{s^3 + 2s^2 + s + 1}\]
\[\boxed{(B) \ \ H(s) = \frac{s^2 + 1}{s^3 + 2s^2 + s + 1}}\]

questions.question: Consider a causal second-order system with the transfer function \[G(s) = \dfrac{1}{1 + 2s + s^2}\] with a unit-step \(R(s) = \dfrac{1}{s}\) as an input. Let \(C(s)\) be the corresponding output. The time taken by the system output \(c(t)\) to reach \(94\%\) of its steady-state value \(\lim\limits_{t \to \infty} c(t)\), rounded off to two decimal places, is
questions.explanation: \[G(s) = \frac{2}{s^2 + 2s + 1} = \frac{1}{(s + 1)^2}\] \[C(s) = G(s)R(s) = \frac{1}{s(s + 1)^2}\] Using partial fraction expansion, we get, \[C(s) = \frac{A}{s} + \frac{B}{(s + 1)} + \frac{C}{(s + 1)^2}\] \[\therefore C(s) = \frac{1}{s} - \frac{1}{(s + 1)} - \frac{1}{(s + 1)^2}\] \[c(t) = (1 - e^{-t} - te^{-t})u(t)\] \[\lim_{t \to \infty} c(t) = 1\] In order to reach \(94\%\) of its steady-state value : \((1 - e^{-t} - te^{-t}) = 0.94\) By trial and error, we get, \[\boxed{(B) \ \ t \approx 4.50\,\text{sec}}\]

questions.question: Consider a unity feedback system, as in the figure shown, with an integral compensator \(\dfrac{K}{s}\) and open-loop transfer function \[G(s) = \frac{1}{s^2 + 3s + 2}\] where \(K > 0\). The positive value of \(K\) for which there are exactly two poles of the unity feedback system on the \(j\omega\) axis is equal to (rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Given, \[G(s)=\frac{1}{s^2+3s+2}\] The compensator is \[\frac{K}{s}\] Therefore, the open loop transfer function becomes \[G_{OL}(s)=\frac{K}{s(s^2+3s+2)}\] For unity feedback systems, \[1+G_{OL}(s)=0\] \[1+\frac{K}{s(s^2+3s+2)}=0\] \[s(s^2+3s+2)+K=0\] \[s^3+3s^2+2s+K=0\] The question asks for the value of \(K\) for which there are exactly two poles on the \(j\omega\)-axis. This corresponds to the condition of marginal stability. Hence, we use the Routh criterion. Constructing the Routh array, \[\begin{array}{c|cc}
s^3 & 1 & 2\\
s^2 & 3 & K\\ s^1 & \dfrac{6-K}{3} & 0\\ s^0 & K & \\
\end{array}\] For marginal stability, one complete row must become zero. Therefore, \[\frac{6-K}{3}=0\] \[6-K=0\] \[K=6\] To verify that the roots actually lie on the \(j\omega\)-axis, form the auxiliary equation using the row just above the zero row. The auxiliary equation is obtained from the \(s^2\) row: \[3s^2+6=0\] \[s^2+2=0\] \[s=\pm j\sqrt{2}\] Hence, two poles lie on the imaginary axis. Therefore, the value of \(K\) is: \[\boxed{6}\]

questions.question: A linear Hamming code is used to map \(4\)-bit messages to \(7\)-bit codewords. The encoder mapping is linear. If the message \(0001\) is mapped to the codeword \(0000111\), and the message \(0011\) is mapped to the codeword \(1100110\), then the message \(0010\) is mapped to
questions.explanation: Theory: For a linear block code, the modulo-2 sum (XOR) of two valid messages maps to the modulo-2 sum of their corresponding codewords. Given, \[0001 \longrightarrow 0000111\]and \[0011 \longrightarrow 1100110.\]Since the encoder is linear, \[0010 = 0011 \oplus 0001.\]Therefore, the corresponding codeword is \[c(0010) = c(0011)\oplus c(0001).\]Substituting the given codewords, \[c(0010) = 1100110 \oplus 0000111.\]Performing bitwise XOR, \[\begin{array}{ccccccc} 1&1&0&0&1&1&0\\ \oplus&&&&&&\\ 0&0&0&0&1&1&1\\ \hline 1&1&0&0&0&0&1 \end{array}\]Hence, \[c(0010)=1100001.\]Therefore, \[\boxed{(B)1100001}\]

questions.question: A single bit, equally likely to be \(0\) and \(1\), is to be sent across an additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel with power spectral density \(N_0/2\). Binary signaling, with \(0\mapsto p(t)\) and \(1\mapsto q(t)\), is used for the transmission, along with an optimal receiver that minimizes the bit-error probability. Let \(\varphi_1(t),\varphi_2(t)\) form an orthonormal signal set. If we choose \(p(t)=\varphi_1(t)\) and \(q(t)=-\varphi_1(t)\), we would obtain a certain bit-error probability \(P_b\). If we keep \(p(t)=\varphi_1(t)\), but take \(q(t)=\sqrt{E}\,\varphi_2(t)\), for what value of \(E\) would we obtain the same bit-error probability \(P_b\)?
questions.explanation: Theory: For optimum binary detection in AWGN, the bit-error probability depends only on the Euclidean distance between the two signal points. Therefore, to obtain the same \(P_b\), the minimum distance \(d_{\min}\) must remain unchanged. Case 1: Given, \[p(t)=\phi_1(t), \qquad q(t)=-\phi_1(t).\]The corresponding signal points are located at [figure unavailable] \[(+1,0) \quad \text{and} \quad (-1,0).\]Hence, the Euclidean distance between them is \[d_{\min} = \sqrt{(1-(-1))^2} = 2.\] Case 2: Now, \[p(t)=\phi_1(t), \qquad q(t)=\sqrt{E}\,\phi_2(t).\]The signal points are \[(1,0) \quad \text{and} \quad (0,\sqrt{E}).\]Therefore, \[d_{\min} = \sqrt{(1-0)^2+\left(0-\sqrt{E}\right)^2} = \sqrt{1+E}.\] [figure unavailable] For the same bit-error probability, \[d_{\min} \text{ must be the same in both cases.}\]Hence, \[\sqrt{1+E}=2.\]Squaring both sides, \[1+E=4.\] Therefore, \[\boxed{(D)3}\]

questions.question: A voice signal \(m(t)\) is in the frequency range \(5\) kHz to \(15\) kHz. The signal is amplitude-modulated to generate an AM signal \(f(t)=A(1+m(t))\cos 2\pi f_c t,\) where \(f_c=600\) kHz. The AM signal \(f(t)\) is to be digitized and archived. This is done by first sampling \(f(t)\) at \(1.2\) times the Nyquist frequency, and then quantizing each sample using a \(256\)-level quantizer. Finally, each quantized sample is binary coded using \(K\) bits, where \(K\) is the minimum number of bits required for the encoding. The rate, in Megabits per second (rounded off to \(2\) decimal places), of the resulting stream of coded bits is Mbps.
questions.explanation: Theory: The coded bit rate is equal to the sampling rate multiplied by the number of bits used to represent each quantized sample. The message signal occupies the frequency range \[5~\text{kHz} \leq f \leq 15~\text{kHz}.\]The carrier frequency is \[f_c = 600~\text{kHz}.\]Hence, the AM signal occupies the frequency band \[f_c - 15~\text{kHz} \;\; \text{to} \;\; f_c + 15~\text{kHz}\] \[= 585~\text{kHz} \;\; \text{to} \;\; 615~\text{kHz}.\]Therefore, the highest frequency component present is \[f_{\max}=615~\text{kHz}.\] [figure unavailable] The Nyquist sampling rate is \[f_N = 2f_{\max}\] \[= 2(615~\text{kHz})\] \[=1230~\text{kHz} =1.23~\text{MHz}.\]Since sampling is performed at \(1.2\) times the Nyquist rate, \[f_s = 1.2f_N\] \[=1.2\times 1.23\] \[=1.476~\text{MHz}.\]A \(256\)-level quantizer requires \[K=\log_2(256)=8\]bits per sample. Hence, the coded bit rate is \[R_b = Kf_s\] \[=8\times 1.476\]Therefore, \[\boxed{ R_b = 11.81~\text{Mbps} }\]

questions.question:
A random variable \(X\) takes values \(-1\) and \(+1\) with probabilities \(0.2\) and \(0.8\), respectively. It is transmitted across a channel which adds noise \(N\), so that the random variable at the channel output is \(Y=X+N.\) The noise \(N\) is independent of \(X\), and is uniformly distributed over the interval \([-2,2]\). The receiver makes a decision \[\hat{X}=
\begin{cases}
-1, & \text{if } Y\leq \theta \\
+1, & \text{if } Y>\theta
\end{cases}\] where the threshold \(\theta\in[-1,1]\) is chosen so as to minimize the probability of error \(\Pr[\hat{X}\neq X]\). The minimum probability of error, rounded off to \(1\) decimal place, is .
questions.explanation: Theory: To minimize the probability of error, the receiver should use the MAP (Maximum A Posteriori) decision rule. Given, \[P(X=+1)=0.8, \qquad P(X=-1)=0.2.\]The noise \(N\) is uniformly distributed over \[[-2,2].\]Hence, \[f_N(n)=\frac{1}{4}, \qquad -2\le n\le 2.\]Since \[Y=X+N,\]the conditional densities are \[f_Y(y|X=+1)=\frac{1}{4}, \qquad -1\le y\le 3,\]and \[f_Y(y|X=-1)=\frac{1}{4}, \qquad -3\le y\le 1.\] [figure unavailable] The overlap region of the two densities is \[-1\le y\le 1.\]In the overlap region, \[f_Y(y|+1)P(+1) = \frac{1}{4}(0.8) = 0.2,\] \[f_Y(y|-1)P(-1) = \frac{1}{4}(0.2) = 0.05.\]Since \[0.2>0.05,\]the MAP rule always favors \[X=+1\]throughout the overlap region. Therefore, the optimum threshold is placed at the left edge of the overlap region: \[\boxed{\theta=-1}.\] Now, an error occurs only when \[X=-1\]is transmitted but the receiver decides \[X=+1.\]That is, \[P_e = P(X=-1)\, P(Y>-1\,|\,X=-1).\]For \(X=-1\), \[Y \sim \text{Uniform}[-3,1].\]Hence, \[P(Y>-1\,|\,X=-1) = \frac{1-(-1)}{1-(-3)} = \frac{2}{4} = \frac{1}{2}.\]Therefore, \[P_e = 0.2\times\frac{1}{2} = 0.1.\]Thus, the minimum probability of error is \[\boxed{ P_{e,\min}=0.1 }\]

questions.ref: Coordinate Geometry & Maxwell's Equation - Basics Q1
questions.question:
In the table shown, List-I and List-II respectively, contain terms appearing on the left-hand side and the right-hand side of Maxwell's equations (in their standard form). Match the left-hand side withe the corresponding right-hand side.
List-IList-II
1. \( abla \cdot \vec{D}\)P. \(0\)
2. \( abla imes \vec{E}\)Q. \( ho\)
3. \( abla \cdot \vec{B}\)R. \(-\dfrac{\partial \vec{B}}{\partial t}\)
4. \( abla imes \vec{H}\)S. \(\vec{J} + \dfrac{\partial \vec{D}}{\partial t}\)
questions.explanation:
The Maxwell's equations in differential form (point form) for time-varying fields as shown in the image are: \[ abla \cdot \vec{D} = ho_{v}\] \[ abla imes \vec{E} = -\dfrac{\partial \vec{B}}{\partial t}\] \[ abla \cdot \vec{B} = 0\] \[ abla imes \vec{H} = \vec{J} + \dfrac{\partial \vec{D}}{\partial t}\]These four equations form the foundation of classical electromagnetism, describing how electric and magnetic fields are generated and altered by each other and by charges and currents. \[ oxed{ ext{(D) Maxwell's Equations}}\]
Key points
  • Gauss's Law for Electricity: \( abla \cdot \vec{D} = ho_{v}\) states that electric charge density is the source of the electric displacement field.
  • Faraday's Law of Induction: \( abla imes \vec{E} = -\dfrac{\partial \vec{B}}{\partial t}\) describes how a time-varying magnetic field induces an electric field.
  • Gauss's Law for Magnetism: \( abla \cdot \vec{B} = 0\) indicates that there are no magnetic monopoles; magnetic field lines are continuous loops.
  • Ampere-Maxwell Law: \( abla imes \vec{H} = \vec{J} + \dfrac{\partial \vec{D}}{\partial t}\) shows that magnetic fields are generated by electric currents and time-varying electric displacement fields (displacement current).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Ensure that the partial derivative \(\dfrac{\partial}{\partial t}\) is used for time-varying fields, rather than a total derivative, when dealing with the point form.
  • Do not confuse the conduction current density \(\vec{J}\) with the displacement current density \(\vec{J}_{d} = \dfrac{\partial \vec{D}}{\partial t}\).

questions.question: The dispersion equation of a waveguide, which relates the wave number '\(k\)' to the frequency \(\omega\), is \(k(\omega) = \left(\dfrac{1}{c}\right)\sqrt{\omega^2 - \omega_0^2}\) where the speed of light \(c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}\), and \(\omega_0\) is a constant. If the group velocity is \(2 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}\), then the phase velocity is
questions.explanation:
The relationship between phase velocity \(v_{p}\) and group velocity \(v_{g}\) is derived from the dispersion relation \(k(\omega) = \frac{1}{c} \sqrt{\omega^{2} - \omega_{0}^{2}}\).
  • Phase Velocity (\(v_{p}\)):
    \[v_{p} = \frac{\omega}{\beta} = \frac{\omega}{k} = \frac{c}{\sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{\omega_{0}}{\omega}\right)^{2}}}\]
  • Group Velocity (\(v_{g}\)):
    By definition, \(v_{g} = \frac{d\omega}{dk} = \left(\frac{dk}{d\omega}\right)^{-1}\). \[\frac{dk}{d\omega} = \frac{1}{c} \cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\omega^{2} - \omega_{0}^{2}}} \cdot 2\omega = \frac{\omega}{c\sqrt{\omega^{2} - \omega_{0}^{2}}}\] \[v_{g} = c \sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{\omega_{0}}{\omega}\right)^{2}}\]
Multiplying the two expressions confirms the product is constant: \[v_{p} \cdot v_{g} = c^{2}\] Given \(c = 3 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}\) and \(v_{g} = 2 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}\): \[v_{p} = \frac{c^{2}}{v_{g}} = \frac{(3 \times 10^{8})^{2}}{2 \times 10^{8}} = \frac{9 \times 10^{16}}{2 \times 10^{8}}\] \[v_{p} = 4.5 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}\] \[\boxed{(D):4.5 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}}\]
Key points
  • In dispersive media (like waveguides), the relationship \(v_{p} v_{g} = c^{2}\) holds true.

questions.question: A rectangular waveguide of width '\(w\)' and height '\(h\)' has cut-off frequencies for \(\text{TE}_{10}\) and \(\text{TE}_{11}\) modes in the ratio \(1 : 2\). The aspect ratio \(w/h\), rounded off to two decimal places, is ____.
questions.explanation:
The general formula for the cut-off frequency \(f_{c}\) of a \(TE_{mn}\) mode in a rectangular waveguide with width \(w\) and height \(h\) is: \[f_{c,mn} = \frac{c}{2} \sqrt{\left(\frac{m}{w}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{n}{h}\right)^{2}}\] For the \(TE_{10}\) mode (\(m=1, n=0\)): \[f_{c,10} = \frac{c}{2w} \quad \dots(\text{i})\] For the \(TE_{11}\) mode (\(m=1, n=1\)): \[f_{c,11} = \frac{c}{2} \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{w}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{1}{h}\right)^{2}} = \frac{c}{2w} \sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{w}{h}\right)^{2}} \quad \dots(\text{ii})\] Given the ratio of the cut-off frequencies: \[\frac{f_{c,10}}{f_{c,11}} = \frac{1}{2} \quad \dots(\text{iii})\] Substituting (i) and (ii) into (iii): \[\frac{\frac{c}{2w}}{\frac{c}{2w} \sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{w}{h}\right)^{2}}} = \frac{1}{2}\] \[\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{w}{h}\right)^{2}}} = \frac{1}{2}\] Squaring both sides: \[1 + \left(\frac{w}{h}\right)^{2} = 4\] \[\left(\frac{w}{h}\right)^{2} = 3\] \[\frac{w}{h} = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.732\] \[\boxed{1.732}\]
Key points
  • The cut-off frequency determines the range of frequencies that can propagate through a waveguide mode.
  • \(TE_{mn}\) modes are transverse electric modes where the electric field is purely transverse to the direction of propagation.

questions.question: Radiation resistance of a small dipole current element of length \(l\) at a frequency of \(3 \text{ GHz}\) is \(3 \text{ }\Omega\). If the length is changed by \(1\%\), then the percentage change in the radiation resistance, rounded off to two decimal places, is \(\%\).
questions.explanation:
The radiation resistance \(R_{rad}\) of a small dipole current element of length \(l\) is given by the formula: \[R_{rad} = 80 \pi^2 \left( \frac{l}{\lambda} \right)^2\] From this expression, it is evident that the radiation resistance is proportional to the square of the length: \[R_{rad} \propto l^2\] Consequently, for two different lengths \(l_1\) and \(l_2\), the ratio of their radiation resistances \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) is: \[\frac{R_2}{R_1} = \left( \frac{l_2}{l_1} \right)^2\] Given that the length is increased by \(1\%\), we have \(l_2 = 1.01 l_1\). Substituting this into the ratio: \[\frac{R_2}{R_1} = \left( \frac{1.01 l_1}{l_1} \right)^2 = (1.01)^2 = 1.0201\] The percentage change in radiation resistance is calculated as: \[\text{Percentage Change} = \left( \frac{R_2 - R_1}{R_1} \right) \times 100\] \[= \left( \frac{R_2}{R_1} - 1 \right) \times 100\] \[= (1.0201 - 1) \times 100 = 0.0201 \times 100 = 2.01\%\] \[\boxed{2.01}\]
Key points
  • For electrically small dipoles (\(l \ll \lambda\)), the radiation resistance increases quadratically with element length.
  • This relationship is fundamental in calculating antenna efficiency and impedance matching requirements.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse the square relationship (\(R \propto l^2\)) with a linear one; neglecting the square will lead to an incorrect result of \(1\%\).
  • Ensure the percentage change formula is applied correctly to the ratio of resistances rather than simply squaring the percentage change of the length.

questions.question: _____ I permitted him to leave, I wouldn't have had any problem with him being absent, ________ I?
questions.explanation:
This is a Past Perfect Conditional sentence pattern. \[\underbrace{\text{Had} + V_3 \text{ form}}_{\text{If clause}}, \quad \underbrace{\text{would have} + V_3 \text{ form}}_{\text{main clause}}\] Had, I permitted him to leave, I wouldn't have had any problem. Negative statement requires affirmative question tag, so would I? \[\boxed{\text{C) Had, would}}\]
Key points
  • Past perfect conditional: Had + \(V_3\) in if-clause; would have + \(V_3\) in main clause.
  • Question tags follow the rule: negative statement \(\Rightarrow\) affirmative tag.
  • ``Wouldn't have had'' is negative \(\Rightarrow\) tag must be affirmative ``would I''.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse ``Have'' (present) with ``Had'' (past perfect) in conditional sentences.
  • Do not use a negative tag after a negative statement.

questions.question: Under a certain legal system, prisoners are allowed to make one statement. If their statement turns out to be true then they are hanged. If the statement turns out to be false then they are shot. One prisoner made a statement and the judge had no option but to set him free. Which one of the following could be that statement?
options: I did not commit the crime
questions.explanation:
Under the given legal system:
  • If statement is true \(\Rightarrow\) prisoner is hanged.
  • If statement is false \(\Rightarrow\) prisoner is shot.
Analyse option (c): ``I will be shot.''
  • If the statement is true \(\Rightarrow\) he should be hanged, but the statement says he will be shot — contradiction.
  • If the statement is false \(\Rightarrow\) he should be shot, which makes the statement true — contradiction.
Since both cases lead to contradictions, the judge has no option but to set him free. \[\boxed{\text{C) I will be shot}}\]
